questions.prompt: Explain how Atlas makes time an input instead of something code reads. Where is the real clock created and how does it reach the code that needs it, how does a calendar 'today' get into a domain rule such as probation, what exactly does the ambient-time fitness function check and what would slip past it, and which time-zone residual did the team leave on purpose?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The system clock is registered exactly once, at composition, as the TimeProvider singleton; every use case and adapter downstream receives a TimeProvider through its constructor, which is the single seam a test replaces to freeze time.

[w3] Domain rules take the date as a parameter: the probation check became a pure question about a given DateOnly, and the API derives that date once from the injected provider and passes it into the projection, so the same worker gives the same answer for the same date on any server.

[w3] The rule has teeth because the build enforces it: a domain test walks every source file of the domain project, skips generated obj/ output and strips comments, and breaks the build with a file:line list for every static clock read it finds.

[w2] The pattern names four reads only — Now and UtcNow on DateTime and on DateTimeOffset — so other ambient sources such as DateTime.Today, TimeProvider.System or a Stopwatch in domain code would pass; the ban is narrower than 'no ambient time' and a reviewer still has to watch for those.
[w1] Comments are stripped before matching so a WHY-comment may name the banned APIs, but string literals are not, so even a string mentioning a banned read fails a domain file.
[w2] A ban instead of a one-line patch, because switching that line to a UTC read would have fixed the incident and left the next convenient static clock free to appear.
keyPoints.quote: Fixes one line, not the class of bug.

keyPoints.text: [w2] The deliberate residual: 'today' is still derived in UTC, not in the worker's own calendar, because Atlas does not model a worker time zone yet; for a worker in UTC+8 the two dates can differ, and the code and a sprint exercise say so.
keyPoints.quote: For a Manila worker, "today" in UTC can differ from "today" in UTC+8.

questions.prompt: Walk through what makes Atlas's date-dependent behaviour deterministic under test: how a money-moving use case treats 'now' within one operation, how tests pin time, how 'which terms applied on date X' is answered and why arrival order does not matter, what keeps one record per worker per day true under concurrent requests, why the leave balance has no column, and how a lockout window can be tested without waiting.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Read the clock once per operation: PayInvoice takes a single 'now' before calling the provider and uses that same instant for the invoice transition, the audit entry and the published event, so every record of one payment agrees on when it happened.
[w3] Tests pass a TimeProvider subclass that always returns one chosen instant, so 'created just now' becomes an exact equality instead of a range that ages.

[w2] Terms on a date are a pure fold over history: among records whose EffectiveFrom is on or before the date, the latest wins, with creation time as the tie-break so the function is total over any list a test builds; shuffling the input cannot change the answer.
[w2] The domain's same-day check only produces a friendly business-rule answer; a unique index on worker and EffectiveFrom is what keeps one record per worker per day true when two requests race.

[w3] The leave balance is recomputed on every read from policy, hire date and approved requests, so there is no second copy that concurrent writes could let drift; the cost is a small recomputation per read.
keyPoints.quote: A leave balance is a pure function of `policy + hireDate + approved requests`.

keyPoints.text: [w2] A reconciliation property test pins that claim instead of a stored balance: the balance re-derived from the request ledger must equal the engine's answer, and available leave never exceeds entitlement plus carryover.
keyPoints.quote: re-deriving the balance from the request ledger equals what the engine

keyPoints.text: [w1] The login lockout decision is a pure policy over the attempt state and an instant; the in-memory adapter only feeds it the injected clock's time, so tests step through a lockout window with explicit instants instead of sleeping.

questions.prompt: Explain the Idempotency-Key middleware and the error contract as seams: which requests the middleware even considers and why authentication comes first, what it fingerprints and what it remembers, why the storage behind it is a port, what happens when two requests with the same key arrive at the same moment, and how each failure family reaches the client.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Only POSTs from a caller with an org are considered: keys are scoped per org, and an anonymous request flows on to the endpoint so its authentication answers first, instead of being told to add a header before it has even logged in.

[w2] The fingerprint is a SHA-256 over method, path and body, compared in constant time with the stored one; a key seen before with the same fingerprint replays the stored response instead of running the endpoint again, while the same key with a different fingerprint is refused rather than masked.
[w2] A response is remembered only when its status is in the success range, and its timestamp comes from the injected clock; a failed or unavailable answer leaves the key free for an honest retry.

[w3] The store is a port in the application layer, so the middleware never depends on EF; the EF adapter works through its own short-lived context so that recording a response can never flush a use case's tracked changes, and a test can swap in any implementation.

[w3] Two requests with the same key at the same moment both look up nothing and both run the endpoint; the unique (org, key) index then rejects the second record and the store swallows that error. The middleware therefore stops sequential retries, not simultaneous ones, and the use case still has to be safe on its own.

[w3] One translation table maps the application's exception families to status codes and problem types, so no endpoint invents its own; anything not in the table is deliberately left to become a 500 that pages someone rather than a smoothed-over 4xx.

[w2] A provider that cannot be reached is not a failed payment: the use case leaves the invoice untouched and raises a dedicated exception that the table turns into a retry signal, so reconciliation never sees a failure that did not happen.
